title: Jamie Dimon Just Said 5 Words Blocking Outside AI Agents From JPMorgan Accounts: "You Don't Want Rogue Agents." Here's Why That Security Stance Matters for JPM and Its Tech Rivals. - The Motley Fool
content: The CEO of JPMorgan Chase isn't going to open his customers' accounts to "just any" AI agents from third parties. Agentic AI is often described as the next wave of artificial intelligence (AI) technology. With AI agents, people can use AI to automate various tasks for them, at work and in their personal lives. A prominent recent example is Meta Platforms (META +2.90%), which made a big splash in September with the launch of Muse, its personal AI agent. Meta's Muse is designed to help people offload some of their everyday online tasks, like sending emails, filling out forms, booking travel, and even shopping. It reached the rare milestone of 10 million downloads after only 40 days on the market and was widely praised for its ease of use and making agentic AI "real" for consumers. If users give permission and access to their banking and credit card data, Muse can even help people with financial tasks and managing money, like setting a budget, negotiating bills, or canceling unwanted subscriptions. But what if banks don't allow Muse (or other AI agents) to connect to their customers' accounts? There are cybersecurity and liability questions involved with allowing people to use AI agents for sensitive financial tasks like managing a bank account, trading stocks, or making credit card payments. Not every bank is on board with this. Last month on the bank's quarterly earnings call, Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase (JPM +0.98%), sounded a five-word warning about the future of AI agents for banking. He said, "You don't want rogue agents." Let's look at what Dimon's remarks might mean for AI agents -- and why JPMorgan Chase is not the only company figuring out how to accept outside AI agents. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. Image source: JPMorgan Chase & Co. Banks must follow strict regulations called "Know Your Customer" rules. That means banks are required to know who is accessing an account, who is authorizing a transaction, and other details to identify customers to help prevent financial fraud and money laundering. AI agents could potentially bring complexity and added risk to banks' "Know Your Customer" compliance. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,116,882 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. What if an AI agent "goes rogue" and makes an unauthorized transaction, or is used to commit financial crimes? What if an AI agent gets into a part of the customer's account that the customer didn't allow? What if a customer later claims that a purchase was fraudulent, even though the customer allowed their AI agent to execute the transaction? Most banks would rather not deal with these hassles and extra risks. Allowing third-party agents like Meta Muse might create liabilities for banks and their customers that banks can't control and didn't choose. On the October earnings call, Jamie Dimon also said that at JPMorgan Chase, "we are not gonna allow just any agent to come, outside agent to come inside the company because it is just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan." On Wednesday, United Airlines(UAL -1.74%) announced that it is restricting access for unauthorized third-party AI agents or assistants. The airline's statement referred to the risks of AI agents causing unauthorized bookings, unintended usage of airline frequent flyer miles, and possible violations of FAA and DOT safety regulations for airline passengers. United Airlines is another example of a business in a heavily regulated industry that must manage sensitive transactions and confidential customer data. And they're tapping the brakes on AI agents. If other banks and airlines adopt this same security-oriented stance, the future of personal agentic AI for companies like Meta Platforms might become less user-friendly -- and less profitable. A transcript of the session has since been posted by Seeking Alpha, giving market participants a record of the discussion. The update keeps JPMorgan Chase firmly on the radar of investors tracking Financial Stocks. The conference slot came several weeks after the bank delivered quarterly results that showed net earnings of many of dollars and revenue up in the high single digits from a year earlier, as summarized by Pulse 2. Shares of JPMorgan Chase trade on the New York Stock Exchange, which places the stock in the NYSE Composite, and it is also a constituent of the S&P 500, the [Dow Jones Industrial Average] and the Russell 1000. Those numbers set the backdrop against which the Boston audience gauged how the bank sees deposit costs, lending demand, expenses and capital for the final months of the year. The BancAnalysts Association of Boston gathering is among the longer-running fixtures on the bank calendar, and JPMorgan Chase has appeared there regularly for years, with transcripts of earlier sessions posted on the bank's IR site. Because the event lands in the middle of the final quarter, it tends to serve as a checkpoint between the October earnings call and the January report. According to the summary published by Pulse 2, JPMorgan Chase reported quarterly net earnings of many of dollars, with revenue rising by a high-single-digit rate compared with the same quarter a year earlier. The same report described core businesses as strengthening, a characterization that covered both the consumer franchise and the corporate and markets operations. Net interest revenue, the spread the bank earns between what it collects on loans and securities and what it pays on deposits and borrowings, remains the single largest driver of JPMorgan Chase's top line. Its trajectory depends on the path of short-term rates set by the Federal Reserve, on deposit pricing and on loan growth. JPMorgan Chase reports through several main segments: Consumer and Community Banking, the combined corporate and markets franchise, and Asset and Wealth Management. Each had a role in the latest quarter, according to the earnings summaries, and each feeds into what the bank can say about the current quarter. In the trading session ahead of the Boston event, JPMorgan Chase shares fell modestly, according to ad-hoc-news. The outlet did not attribute the decline to a single company-specific trigger, and moves of that size in large bank stocks often reflect broader shifts in rate expectations or in appetite for the sector as a whole. JPMorgan Chase has for several years run among the largest technology budgets in global banking, with spending directed at cloud migration, payments infrastructure, cybersecurity and, increasingly, artificial-intelligence tools. Management has argued that this spending supports long-term efficiency and competitive position, even as it keeps headline expenses elevated. The decision to block outside AI agents from directly operating customer accounts, reported by CNBC last month, sits alongside the conference appearance as part of a broader debate about how large banks approach automation. Agent software that can log in, move money or pay bills on a customer's behalf offers convenience, but it also opens new paths for fraud and errors that banks would ultimately be asked to resolve. The next major scheduled milestone is final-quarter and full-year earnings release, which the bank typically issues in mid-January as the first of the large US lenders to report. That release will include updated guidance on net interest revenue and expenses for the coming year.
